title: Obligations of importers, distributors and deployers of high-risk AI systems under the AI Act
explain_beginner: The European Union's AI Act creates rules for different companies involved in selling and using high-risk artificial intelligence systems. This paper explains what each company must do. Importers and distributors mainly verify that products meet safety standards, while companies actually using the AI have separate responsibilities for managing risks during operation. Interestingly, if someone modifies an AI system, they may suddenly face the same strict rules as the original maker. Understanding these different roles matters because it helps everyone avoid penalties and reduces dangers from AI systems.
explain_business: Organizations must understand their specific role in AI supply chains under EU regulations to avoid substantial fines. Importers face more demanding compliance verification than distributors, while companies deploying AI systems carry distinct accountability for managing risks during use. A key practical insight is that modifying purchased AI systems can create full provider-level compliance obligations. This means companies should audit whether their modifications trigger enhanced responsibilities. Clear identification of supply chain roles and potential obligation shifts is critical for compliance strategy, financial planning, and operational risk management across European markets.
explain_practitioner: This work analyzes EU AI Act compliance obligations across the supply chain for high-risk systems. Importers perform primary verification of provider compliance while distributors have narrower verification duties. Deployers carry independent, non-subordinate obligations focused on operational risks rather than design compliance. The analysis identifies a critical scenario where modifications to AI systems trigger provider-equivalent obligations on actors who were not original deployers. This stems from AI susceptibility to purpose drift independent of original design intent. Clarifying these distinctions across importers, distributors, and deployers is essential for regulatory compliance and risk mitigation.
